actions.reason: Neither change got close to the 0.9900 bar. Both gave identical outputs. (1) Counting the neighbour pairs in BasicTokenizer.train with C-level Counter/filter/itemgetter, plus making the RegexTokenizer.train pair index a defaultdict(list): train_ir went from 330077592 to 330095548, ratio 1.0001. (2) Adding a dict.fromkeys de-duplication of the chunks visited on each merge: ratio 1.0045. The per-merge Python loops in both train methods now seem to be a small share of train_ir. Most of the count looks like fixed cost (interpreter startup, importing and compiling regex, corpus generation), but I haven't profiled that split. All edits are reverted.

worker_outcome: no candidate: the session stopped without submitting a change [stop: gave up; model calls: 12]

journal.text:
I tried two changes to train speed in minbpe, measured as train_ir. First, in BasicTokenizer.train I counted neighbour pairs with Counter, filter and itemgetter, and in RegexTokenizer.train I made the pair index a defaultdict(list). Second, I added a dict.fromkeys de-duplication of the chunks visited on each merge.

Both builds passed and outputs were identical. The first change moved train_ir from 330077592 to 330095548, ratio 1.0001, against a required 0.9900. encode_ir went to 0.9972. The second change gave train_ir 331552095, ratio 1.0045, so it was worse. encode_ir was 0.9973. Neither change helped. I submitted no candidate.

Swapping Python loops for C-level helpers in these train functions does not move the instruction count. The cost seems to sit in the per-merge work itself, not in how pairs are counted or indexed.

Next I would profile RegexTokenizer.train per merge before editing. I would look for a change that skips work on each merge, not one that does the same work faster.
